chunks: From him, from one of his companions from the Iraqis, raising it, said:

Al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him) addressed the people, so he said: 'O people! I am informing you about a brother of mine who was among the greatest of people in my eyes, and the foremost reason for his greatness in my eyes was his belittling of the world in his eyes.'

He was outside the control of his belly, so he did not desire what he did not find, nor did he indulge excessively when he found it. He was outside the control of his private part, so it did not diminish his intellect and his opinion. He was outside the control of ignorance, so he did not extend his hand except towards a reliable benefit.

He was neither lustful, nor angry, nor impatient. Most of his lifetime he was silent. So when he spoke, he surpassed the speakers. He did not enter into disputes, nor participate in allegations, nor present an argument until he saw a judge. He was not oblivious to his brethren, nor did he single himself out with anything besides them. He was weak and weakened, but when seriousness came, he was a fierce lion.
He did not blame anyone for what an excuse would be valid for, until he heard the apology. He did what he said, and did what he did not say.

When two matters presented to him, not knowing which was superior, he looked at the one closest to desire and opposed it. He did not complain of a pain except in the presence of one from whom he hoped for a cure, nor did he consult anyone except one from whom he hoped for good advice.
He was not impatient, nor angry, nor complaining, nor lustful, nor revengeful, nor oblivious to the enemy.

So upon you is with the likes of these noble character traits if you can endure them. If you cannot endure all of them, then taking the few is better than leaving the many. And there is no might and no strength except with Allah.
ai.seo_question: What are the key moral characteristics of a righteous person according to Imam Al-Hasan ibn Ali?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi is traditionally interpreted by Shia scholars as describing Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib, presenting him as the ideal model of the 'Momin' through his mastery over the three primary appetites: the belly, the private part, and ignorance. The narrative emphasizes his strategic silence, equitable judgment, and psychological resilience, offering a practical framework for spiritual self-discipline (mujahada) that balances asceticism with active social engagement.

en.hubeali: From him, from one of his companions from the Iraqis, raising it, said,

‘Al-Hassan<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> Bin Ali<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> addressed (the people), so he<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> said: ‘O you people! I<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> am informing you of a brother of mine<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> who was from the greatest of the people in my<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> eyes, and it was so that the topmost of what made him to be the greatest in my<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> eyes was his belittling of the world in his eyes.

He was outside from the grasp of his belly, so he did not desire what he did not find, nor did he frequent it when he did find (it). He was outside the grasp of his private part, so it did not take his intellect and his opinion lightly. He was outside the grasp of the ignorance, so he did not extend his hand except towards a reliable benefit.

It was so that he was neither lustful, nor angry, nor impatient. Most of his lifetime he was silent. So when he did speak, he surpassed the speakers. He neither entered into disputes nor did he participate in allegations, nor did he cast an argument until he saw a judge, and he was not oblivious from his brethren, nor did he specialise himself with anything besides them. He was weak, weakened, so when there was a seriousness, he was an advancing lion.
He did not blame anyone in what the excuse occurred in the likes of it until he saw an apology. He was doing what he was saying and (not do) what he was not saying.

When two matters presented to him, not knowing which of the two was superior, he look at the one closest to the desires, so he opposed it. He did not complain of a pain except in the presence of the one whom he hoped would have a cure for it, nor did he consult anyone except the one he hoped would have good advice with him.
He was neither impatient, nor angry, nor doubtful, nor of lustful desired, nor revengeful, nor was he oblivious from the enemy.

So, upon you is with the likes of these precious mannerisms if you are strong enough for it. But if you cannot endure all of these, so take the few best ones, leave the more. And there is neither a Might nor a Strength except with Allah<sup style="font-weight: normal">azwj</sup>’.
en.sarwar: 26. It is narrated from him (narrator of the Hadith above) from certain individuals of his people from the people of Iraq in a marfu’ manner who has said the following:

“Al-Hassan ibn Ali (a.s.) once addressed the people saying, ‘I like to tell you about one of my friends who was the greatest in my sight. The head of what was the greatest in my sight about him was the worthlessness of the world in his sight.

He was free of the control of his stomach, thus, he did not have any appetite for what he could not find; he, however, would not accede when he did find it. He was out of the control of his private parts and it would not weigh his reason and opinion lightly. He was out of the control of ignorance, thus, he would not extend his hands unless he was confident of its benefits.

He did not desire, become angry, or disappointed. Most of the time he remained silent, and when he spoke, he surpassed the speakers. He did not enter in arguments or take part in claims. He would not testify without the presence of a judge. He was not unaware of his brothers (in belief) and did not appropriate anything for himself without them. He was the weakest of the weak people but in serious matters he acted as an advancing lion.
He did not blame anyone without a good cause. He would do what he said, and would not say what he would not do.

When he became attracted to two things that he did not know which is better he would ignore that which he desired most. He would not complain for any pain before anyone unless he had known that one had a cure for it and would not consult anyone unless he had hope for good advice from him.
He did not become frustrated, angered, and did not complain, desire, revenge and did not remain neglectful of his enemies.
Therefore, you must acquire such noble moral behaviors if you can. You must acquire the little if you cannot bear the whole. There is no means and power without Allah.”’
